related_questions.question: How is child support calculated in WA state?
related_questions.snippet: Washington State uses a child support formula to determine the base monthly child support amount. The factors include the number of children, their ages, and the incomes of the parents. Depending on the variables plugged into the formula, the base child support payment will be anywhere from $200 up to $3,500 per month.

related_questions.question: What are the new child support laws in Washington state?

text_blocks.snippet: Washington State child support laws are primarily governed by the "Income Shares Model," which uses an economic table to calculate obligations based on both parents' net incomes, the number of children, and additional expenses. Recent changes have focused on ensuring low-income parents have enough left over after support payments to meet their basic needs.

text_blocks.snippet: Key Aspects of Washington Child Support Laws:

list.title: Income Shares Model:
list.snippet: Child support is calculated based on both parents' net income, not just the paying parent's income.

list.title: Economic Table:
list.snippet: The law uses a table to determine the basic support obligation based on the combined monthly net income of both parents and the number of children.

list.title: Basic Needs:
list.snippet: Child support is intended to cover the basic needs of the child, including food, clothing, housing, healthcare, and education.

list.title: Minimum Support:
list.snippet: A minimum support amount of $50 per month per child is generally required, but this can be adjusted based on the child's best interests and both parents' financial circumstances.

list.title: Cap on Support:
list.snippet: Generally, neither parent's child support obligation should exceed 45% of their net income unless there are specific circumstances like special needs or a large family.

list.title: High-Income Cases:
list.snippet: For parents with combined monthly net income exceeding $12,000, the court may order an amount above the standard table.

list.title: Modifications:
list.snippet: Child support orders can be modified due to significant life changes, such as changes in income, job loss, or a child's special needs.

list.title: End of Support:
list.snippet: Child support typically ends when the child turns 18 or graduates high school, but there are exceptions for post-secondary education or special needs.

list.title: Incarceration:
list.snippet: Incarcerated parents may be eligible for a temporary reduction in child support payments under certain circumstances, potentially reducing it to $10 per month per child support order.

list.title: Garnishment:
list.snippet: Washington State can intercept child support payments from parents receiving public assistance (TANF).

list.title: Low-Income Adjustments:
list.snippet: The law includes provisions to ensure low-income parents have enough left over after paying support to meet their basic needs.

list.title: Voluntary Underemployment:
list.snippet: Courts can impute income to a parent who is voluntarily underemployed to reduce their child support obligation, but not for a parent who is gainfully employed full-time, unless they are found to be purposely underemployed.

list.title: Rebuttable Presumption of Incapacity:
list.snippet: For parents in court-ordered treatment for a behavioral health disorder, there is a rebuttable presumption that they are unable to pay child support during treatment.

list.title: Changes in 2025:
list.snippet: Lawmakers initially agreed to end the practice of garnishing child support payments from TANF recipients, but later reversed that decision due to budget concerns.

list.title: Abatement:
list.snippet: For incarcerated parents, there are specific procedures for temporary reduction of child support obligations, and the amount gradually increases back to the full amount after release.

list.title: Expansion of Economic Table:
list.snippet: The child support economic table has been expanded to include combined monthly net incomes up to $50,000.

list.title: Review of Low-Income Cases:
list.snippet: For families with income below $1,000 per month, the courts will review expenses and resources individually when determining support obligations.

related_questions.snippet: Key takeaways. By law, both parents must support their children financially. If the parents can't agree on how to share this responsibility, you can ask the court to make a child support order. Child support generally ends when the child turns 18 and graduates from high school, or turns 19, whichever happens first.

text_blocks.snippet: In Washington State, child support is determined using a state-mandated formula that considers both parents' incomes and the number of children. The basic support amount is calculated based on these factors, and there are additional considerations for expenses like childcare and health insurance. Washington State has a specific child support schedule and forms available on the Washington State Courts website.
snippet_highlighted_words: child support is determined using a state-mandated formula that considers both parents' incomes and the number of children

list.title: Income Shares Model:
list.snippet: Washington uses an "income shares" model, meaning the combined parental income is used to determine the total support obligation, and then that obligation is divided proportionally between the parents based on their respective incomes.

list.title: Factors in the Calculation:
list.snippet: The primary factors in the child support calculation are the parents' monthly net incomes and the number of children.

list.title: Basic Support Obligation:
list.snippet: The Washington State Support Schedule provides a table that shows the basic support obligation based on the number of children and combined monthly net income.

list.title: Additional Expenses:
list.snippet: Child support orders may also include provisions for daycare costs, health insurance premiums, and other expenses related to the child's well-being.

list.title: Where to Find Official Information:
list.snippet: The Washington State Courts website provides official forms and instructions for calculating child support. The Washington State Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) also plays a role in child support services.

list.title: Enforcement:
list.snippet: The Washington State Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) handles the enforcement of child support orders.

list.title: Extending Support:
list.snippet: While child support typically ends when a child turns 18 or graduates high school, there are circumstances where it can be extended, such as for post-secondary education.
